title: Connectors and pinouts: USB, PC power, barrels and car sockets
summary: What voltage each common connector gives and how to get power out of salvaged supplies: USB, USB-C Power Delivery, PC power supplies, barrel plugs, laptop chargers, car sockets and battery connectors.

steps.text: Read the label on the power supply: output volts, amps and the polarity symbol.
Measure the output with a meter before you connect anything to it.
Match the voltage exactly. The supply’s current rating must be at least what the device draws; more is fine.
Fuse anything you wire straight to a battery, close to the battery.
steps.warn: A car or lithium battery can deliver hundreds of amps into a short: enough to melt wire and start a fire.

notes:
## USB

| Kind | Gives |
|---|---|
| USB-A and micro-USB chargers | 5 V, 0.5–2.4 A |
| USB-C (plain) | 5 V, up to 3 A |
| USB-C Power Delivery | 5, 9, 15 or 20 V, up to 5 A (100 W); newer chargers 28, 36 or 48 V (240 W) |
| Quick Charge (Qualcomm, USB-A) | 5, 9 or 12 V (some 20 V) |

A Power Delivery charger only raises its voltage when the device asks. A cheap **PD trigger board** does the asking, turning a USB-C charger or power bank into a 9, 15 or 20 V supply for other things (12 V too on chargers that offer it).

USB-A pins: 1 +5 V, 2 data −, 3 data +, 4 ground. The two outer contacts (the longer ones) are power; the two inner ones are data. Check which outer one is + with a meter.

## PC power supply (ATX)

- To run one without a computer, connect the green wire (pin 16 of the 24-pin plug, PS_ON) to any black wire. Unplug it from the wall before you do.
- +12 V comes out on the yellow wires: the 24-pin, the 4- or 8-pin CPU plug, the 6- or 8-pin graphics plugs, Molex and SATA.
- Molex 4-pin: yellow +12 V, black, black, red +5 V.
- SATA power: orange +3.3 V, red +5 V, yellow +12 V.
- Some older supplies won't stay on without a small load on +5 V: a 10 Ω, 10 W resistor across red and black does it.

## Barrel plugs and laptop chargers

- Most are centre positive: check the polarity symbol on the label.
- 5.5 × 2.1 mm and 5.5 × 2.5 mm are the common 12 V sizes (routers, LED strip, cameras, monitors). The two look alike; the wrong one connects badly.
- Laptop chargers are mostly 19–20 V (Dell and HP about 19.5 V, Asus and Acer 19 V, Lenovo 20 V). Read the label. USB-C laptops use Power Delivery.

## Vehicles and batteries

| Connector | Pins |
|---|---|
| Car accessory socket (cigarette lighter) | Centre +12 V, sides ground; usually fused at 10–20 A |
| OBD-II port (under the dash) | Pin 16 battery +12 V (always on), pins 4 and 5 ground |
| Anderson Powerpole | Red +, black −; both halves identical; solar, radio |
| Anderson SB (SB50, SB120…) | The housing colour marks the system voltage, not polarity (forklifts, winches, battery chargers): check polarity with a meter |
| XT60, XT90 | + and − moulded on the plastic; RC, drones, e-bikes |

## Network and mains

- Standard Power over Ethernet (802.3af/at) puts 44–57 V DC on the cable only after the device asks for it. **Passive PoE** (24 or 48 V, common on Ubiquiti and cheap cameras) is always on and can damage ordinary network ports.
- North American 240 V plugs for dryers and stoves carry two live wires. Never adapt one to a 120 V device.
